abstract: Deviations of frequencies and time signals are with respect to the weighted mean of six quartz oscillators, and time signals from WWV over 20-day intervals. articleTitle: Author's reply to discussion
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: To Mr N. M. Georgeson: It must be nearly thirty years ago that Prof. ‘D’ told me how much he suffered from boils on the neck which he had had since world war I. I remarked absent-mindedly that he should give up wearing his radio-active army watch. He did. The boils vanished and he sent me the watch as a present. I handed it back to the Professor some years later at a lecture given in the Physics Laboratory on the dangers of radio-active matter. Prof. ‘D’ never wore the watch again! Mr and Mrs ‘Y’ were engaged some twenty years ago and married 10 years later. They had an MG sports racing car specially fitted with four luminous dials on the dash. Between them the dials gave off over Ir per hour at short range. Mr and Mrs ‘Y’ were proved to be sterile, whilst Mr ‘Y’ has suffered from tummy pains for some years past. Cause not diagnosed!

articleTitle: Vote of thanks
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr L. Axe: Thank you, Mr President. I now call on Mr J. T. Allan to propose a vote of thanks to the President for his address. Mr J. T. Allan (Past President): I consider it a great honour to be called on to propose this vote of thanks. We are all very grateful to Professor Cormack for all he has done during the past 20 odd years to help organize and encourage the work of the laboratory in the University. This description of some of the features of the laboratory will, I hope, encourage members of the Institute to investigate its possibilities further and make use of its facilities.

articleTitle: Some aspects of the stop consonants
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: This paper deals primarily with a study made of the stop consonants, (p, t, k, b, d, g). The importance of extracting the information-bearing qualities of speech is emphasized and an outline is given of the various types of speech sounds and their mode of production. The structure of a stop consonant is given in greater detail. Examples of oscillographic patterns of stop consonants in different contexts are shown. Characteristic features of this type of sound are pointed out and criteria distinguishing the different types of stop consonants formulated. Hypotheses concerning aspects of the production of stop consonants in certain configurations, based on oscillographic evidence, are mentioned briefly. Finally a description is given of experimental apparatus used to separate stop consonants from the rest of speech sounds and thence separate these into voiced and un-voiced types.

articleTitle: Author's reply to discussion
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr Eagle (in reply): I would like to thank the two contributors very much for their remarks. The only things on which I might comment are, first of all, the suggestion that there are other subjects which should possibly go into the engineering syllabus. I myself would like to see more kinetic theory going into the syllabus. I would like to see more solid state go in — and I must emphasize that I have said very little tonight about solid-state devices but that there is a great deal more in the paper, particularly about thermocouples, which I hope will indicate what part the solid-state physicist is playing in the development of devices. I feel the stage is being reached where some consideration of solid-state structure and solid-state properties is an essential part of the engineering course, and it would begin to seem also that some study of plasmas is becoming an essential, or a near essential, feature of a course for engineers, particularly for electrical engineers.

articleTitle: Author's reply to discussion
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Dr Posel (in reply): I thank Professor Heymann for the trouble he has taken in preparing his contribution to the discussion. In reply to his statement that a transient analysis of the parallel-T should have been given ab initio and thereafter the steady-state solution should have been extracted from it, I would like to give the following reasons which advocate, in my opinion, the presentation of the steady-state analysis first. The design of the parallel-T will invariably be approached from the viewpoint of the transfer sensitivity under steady-state conditions, and as a result of these considerations certain restrictions can be placed first on the magnitudes of network components and second, certain combinations of components may be grouped together. As an example of the former there is the finding that the value of R<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</inf> should be made equal to that of R<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf>, and as an example of the latter there arises the combination of network components which was denoted by “d”. Both of these findings emerged from the steady-state analysis and as a result thereof the transient analysis was given in a form more compact than that occurring if the latter investigation had preceded the former. Furthermore, if a reader wishes to use the parallel-T in the application indicated, and if transient analysis per se happens to be not to his liking, the design is accomplished from steady-state considerations with the assurance that the network behaves itself in the transient operation.

articleTitle: Recent developments of A.C. winder control
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Dr E. Friedlander (in reply to Mr P. H. Harvey): I agree with the suggestion that more attention might be given to the reduction of the minimum slip which is possible by means of rotor short-circuiting contactors. The principle has been applied in the past in South Africa as evidenced in the paper by I. B. Stone, (The Certificated Engineer, Sept. 1959). Attention must be given to the last step which, even with a controller reducing the slip to 3 per cent with the electrolyte hot, may produce about 3 times the rated current when the controller is short circuited and correspondingly more when the electrolyte is cold. This tends to emphasize the importance of a wide resistance range for the liquid controller itself also if an economy contactor is to be added.

articleTitle: The measurement and significance of brain rhythms
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: A description is given of the origins of research into the significance of the electroencephalogram (EEG). An account of contemporary recording and analyzing equipment is followed by a brief statement of the salient findings relating to the psychological meaning of these electrical changes in the brain. An explanation of the need for new methods of display leads to a consideration of toposcopic techniques and finally to a description of the apparatus in use in a modern psychophysiological research laboratory.

articleTitle: Voltage regulation by changing transformer tappings on-load
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The extension of electricity supply systems from simple systems serving small towns and communities to the large complex and inter-connected grid systems of today, together with the requirement to maintain a reasonably constant supply voltage at the consumer's terminals, has necessitated the provision of means for varying the voltage ratio of a transformer whilst the transformer is still supplying load. This Paper reviews the requirement of on-load tap changing equipments as regards designs for different applications and contains some remarks on operation and maintenance.

articleTitle: Unconventional methods of generating electrical power
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: A review is given of methods that have been proposed for the ‘direct’ generation of electricity from other forms of energy by methods other than the conventional systems and of experimental devices designed to test the practicability of such proposals. The basic limitations in any energy conversion process are explained and the shortcomings of conventional generation are discussed. Unconventional methods are then classified as: (A) electrochemical conversion, (B) photoelectric conversion, (C) solid-state devices, and (D) use of high-velocity ionized gas. Each of these is discussed in turn, with particular emphasis on trying to give a simple physical explanation of the processes governing the operation of each type of device and of the fundamental limitations to efficiency of conversion in each case. The devices dealt with in particular are fuel cells, solar batteries, thermionic converters, thermocouples (including the plasma diode), and magnetohydrodynamic generators. It is emphasized that the various types are not necessarily competitive, but that each may have a particular sphere of application for which it is most suitable, and that in many cases combinations may prove useful.

articleTitle: Regenerative braking equipment on cape western system of the South African railways
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The purpose of regeneration is reviewed briefly and the various methods of absorbing energy in excess of traction requirements are discussed. The principal reasons for using power dissipating resistor equipment are presented. A brief description of the Cape Western traction electrification follows which includes details of the locomotives used and the method of locomotive control during regenerative braking. The operating requirements of the regenerative braking equipment are stated and details of the various circuits are discussed. Descriptions of the ignitrons and the main resistors follow and a general survey of the equipment is given. An account of the tests carried out on the electronic and power equipment is given and typical results of tests involving locomotives in regenerative combination are reported. The operation of the equipment in service is stated briefly and proposed modifications in design to the present equipment are discussed. A summary of desirable and undesirable features in regenerative braking equipments concludes the paper.

articleTitle: Energy the tenth bernard price memorial lecture
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: “LET US NOW PRAISE FAMOUS MEN,” SAID KIPLING, “who with toil of their To-day, Bought for us Tomorrow”. “For their work continueth, Broad and deep continueth, Great beyond their knowing.” We meet at this Tenth Memorial Lecture to commemorate the life and work of Dr Bernard Price. It is a meet and proper thing so to remind ourselves each year of a man whose personality impressed itself so strongly on the electrical engineering progress of the Union, and on the profession that this Institute represents.

articleTitle: The progress of mass miniature radiography (RP)
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The progress of Mass Miniature Radiography RP (Radiofluorography) since its inception 32 years ago is discussed. The impact of RP on the gold mining industry of South Africa, unique in the world's history, and the peculiar and inexplicable happenings in the new high-speed laboratory are dealt with. Silver recovery and the ‘Law’ are considered and the difference between Strontium 90 fall-out and X-rays applied for diagnostic purposes is explained preceded by an experiment using a luminous watch and a luminous key ring fitting for a car dash-board.

articleTitle: The steady-state and transient response of the unsymmetrical parallel-T network as a transfer bridge used in conjunction with variable-capacitance transducers
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The aim of this paper is to present the unsymmetricai paraliel-T network as an eminently suitable three-terminal transfer bridge for use in conjunction with a variable-capacitance transducer. Design equations based on the steady-state response are formulated and experimental verification thereof is provided. In addition the transient response of the network is analysed in considerable detail for the most severe case of a step change in the transducer capacitance. Finally the application of the apparatus is illustrated via oscillograms to the measurement of the instantaneous pressure in a pipeline subjected to water-hammer action.

articleTitle: Stage and auditorium lighting control
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: ALTHOUGH STAGE AND AUDITORIUM LIGHTING control is a small specialized branch of the general subject of artificial illumination it is, nevertheless, a very important one. The almost explosive rate of expansion of universal cultural progress made during this second half of the twentieth century has resulted in the rapidly increasing frequency and extent of individual contact with the amenities of lighting control. The rapid technological advances which are the dominating features of this cultural expansion are providing improvements in the art of illumination and its control to meet increasingly critical demands. Thus, it is not surprising that some of the techniques in practical use are still novel in principle and application.

articleTitle: Recent developments in A.C. Winder control
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: THE CHOICE OF THE MOTOR AND CONTROL SYSTEM for an electrical winder which years ago would have been dependent on the Ward-Leonard drive is no longer a foregone conclusion for any new winder installation. The Ward-Leonard system, rectifier winders or a.c. drives may be called for today depending on local conditions such as are dictated by depth of shaft, desirable pay load, load limits of the network, susceptibility to harmonics and voltage flicker, climatic conditions, capital costs of electric power, cooling water, buildings and foundations, arrangement of the mechanical installation and mounting of the winder, the types of brakes which may be applicable or preferred, skill of personnel and facilities for maintenance and many more factors must be taken into account if the most suitable solution is to be found for a given case.

articleTitle: An electrical engineering machines laboratory
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: I am very honoured at having been elected as your President. That being so, I am prompted to make the almost customary dedication that I will do my best to further the interests of the Institute in all its activities and to try to maintain the high standard with which our affairs have been conducted in the past. I am conscious that this will be a difficult task, particularly in view of the events of the Jubilee Year which has just passed. This was an outstanding year in all respects, for which the credit must go largely to Mr Rupert Gettliffe who, if I may be allowed to echo sentiments already expressed, worked with energy and zeal to accomplish the desired end. It is my duty now to see that we return to normal whilst at the same time to see that we profit by the spirit which made last year so successful.

articleTitle: The progress of telegraphy
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: THE YEAR 1960 IS THE CENTENARY OF TELEGRAPHS in South Africa for in April, 1860, the first telegraph in the country was opened between Cape Town and Simonstown. It is thus perhaps appropriate to look back over the years to the birth of telegraphy and trace its progress to the present time.

articleTitle: D.E.2 diesel-electric locomotives on the Rhodesia Railways
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: A brief historical introduction and a description of the Salisbury-Umtali system is supported by a discussion on investigations carried out by Rhodesia Railways personnel before embarking upon the first main line railway conversion to diesel-electric motive power. Characteristics and design details of the Class D.E. 2 locomotive are considered and compared with those of steam motive power operating previously on the system. The discussion includes operating data over a period of five years, details of maintenance schedules and a brief comparison of operating costs.

articleTitle: Obituary: Sidney Francis Harvey
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The death of Sidney Francis Harvey, on October 3rd, 1960, at Johannesburg, has removed another of the few remaining pioneers of electricity supply in Southern Africa. He was intimately associated with power requirements in the development of the Witwatersrand gold-fields and surrounding areas. He was born at Richmond, in the County of Surrey, on December 5th, 1877, and came to South Africa with his parents during 1879, receiving his education at Cradock and Kimberley in the Cape Province.

articleTitle: Discussion
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Professor G. R. Bozzoli (Past President): Mr Eagle has presented a topical paper at a very timely moment. Not only is his subject one which follows naturally on last month's Bernard Price Memorial Lecture by Professor M. G. Say, but the subject is “redhot” in the academic as well as the industrial development field. It has been realized for many years that today's fuel resources are far from inexhaustible and the need for thought and action about energy supplies in the future grows rapidly with the march of time. In the first few years of this decade pressure began on the universities to stress this matter and in 1954, at the Conference of Commonwealth Engineering Institutions in London, one of the recommendations was to the effect that the attention of university engineering schools be drawn to the importance of the conservation of natural resources of all kinds. This coincided with the growth of an awareness of the importance of fundamental thought and basic science, and this attitude is well summed up in the views expressed by a number of the major engineering universities in the United States. Typically, Columbia University has set its face against undergraduate specialization and has gone all out to offer fundamental instruction. In 1959, the enrolment in engineering all over the U.S. dropped by 8 000, despite the fact that 50 000 additional young men of university age become available each year. The enrolment in pure science, however, increased by almost exactly the same amount. This is believed to be due to the satellite situation which has turned the scientist into a hero overnight and dropped the engineer back in status to that of a person who takes engines apart!

The association of cultural progress and technical developments in the art and control of illumination are evidenced not only by progress in stage and auditorium lighting control but such developments as the “Son et lumiere” productions in France and proposals for “dynamic lighting” involving a slow continuous variation in intensity and colour of light.
